back: A plant adapted to dry conditions by storing water, reducing water loss or reaching water with deep or wide roots.
Store water (succulents), reach water (deep tap roots), reduce loss (small leaves, spines, waxy cuticle), escape drought (ephemerals), use fog, and tolerate salt (halophytes).
Water is present in the soil but plants cannot take it up, for example because the soil is so salty.
All stores (biomass, litter, soil) and flows are small; decomposition is slow and leaching is low, so the soil holds most nutrients.
A saline soil with a high concentration of soluble salts and often a white surface crust; the pH is usually neutral to slightly alkaline.
A sodic soil with a high proportion of sodium on the clay, strongly alkaline pH, dispersed clay and a dense columnar B horizon.

front: Why salts accumulate in desert soils
back: Evaporation exceeds rainfall, so water moves upwards by capillary rise and evaporates, leaving salts near the surface.
A plant with two strap-like leaves that absorbs moisture from sea fog and can live for hundreds of years.
Salt added (kg per ha) = concentration of salt in water (kg per m³) × volume of water applied (m³ per ha).
